{{Short description|Description of non-logical symbols}}
In [[mathematical logic]], a '''signature''' is a description of the [[non-logical symbol]]s of a [[formal language]]. In [[universal algebra]], a signature lists the operations that characterize an [[algebraic structure]]. In [[model theory]], signatures are used for both purposes. They are rarely made explicit in more philosophical treatments of logic.

==Definition==

Formally, a (single-sorted) '''signature''' can be defined as a 4-tuple <math>\sigma = \left(S_{\operatorname{func}}, S_{\operatorname{rel}}, S_{\operatorname{const}}, \operatorname{ar}\right),</math> where <math>S_{\operatorname{func}}</math> and <math>S_{\operatorname{rel}}</math> are disjoint [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] not containing any other basic logical symbols, called respectively
* ''[[function symbol]]s'' (examples: <math>+, \times</math>),
* ''{{visible anchor|relation symbol}}s'' or ''[[Predicate (mathematical logic) |predicates]]'' (examples: <math>\,\leq, \, \in</math>),
* ''[[constant symbol]]s'' (examples: <math>0, 1</math>),
and a function <math>\operatorname{ar} : S_{\operatorname{func}} \cup S_{\operatorname{rel}} \to \N</math> which assigns a natural number called ''[[arity]]'' to every function or relation symbol. A function or relation symbol is called <math>n</math>-ary if its arity is <math>n.</math> Some authors define a nullary (<math>0</math>-ary) function symbol as ''constant symbol'', otherwise constant symbols are defined separately.

A signature with no function symbols is called a '''{{visible anchor|relational signature}}''', and a signature with no relation symbols is called an '''{{visible anchor|algebraic signature}}'''.<ref name="FastN-Gram-BasedStringSearch">{{cite web |last1=Mokadem |first1=Riad |author2=Litwin, Witold |author3=Rigaux, Philippe |author4=Schwarz, Thomas |title=Fast nGram-Based String Search Over Data Encoded Using Algebraic Signatures |url=http://www.cse.scu.edu/~tschwarz/Papers/vldb07_final.pdf |website=33rd International Conference on Very Large Data Bases (VLDB) |accessdate=27 February 2019 |format=PDF |date=September 2007}}</ref>
A ''{{visible anchor|finite signature}}'' is a signature such that <math>S_{\operatorname{func}}</math> and <math>S_{\operatorname{rel}}</math> are [[Finite set|finite]]. More generally, the ''cardinality'' of a signature <math>\sigma = \left(S_{\operatorname{func}}, S_{\operatorname{rel}}, S_{\operatorname{const}}, \operatorname{ar}\right)</math> is defined as <math>|\sigma| = \left|S_{\operatorname{func}}\right| + \left|S_{\operatorname{rel}}\right| + \left|S_{\operatorname{const}}\right|.</math>

The ''{{visible anchor|language of a signature}}'' is the set of all well formed sentences built from the symbols in that signature together with the symbols in the logical system.

==Other conventions==

In universal algebra the word '''{{visible anchor|type}}''' or '''{{visible anchor|similarity type}}''' is often used as a synonym for "signature". In model theory, a signature <math>\sigma</math> is often called a '''{{visible anchor|vocabulary}}''', or identified with the [[first-order language|(first-order) language]] <math>L</math> to which it provides the [[non-logical symbols]]. However, the [[cardinality]] of the language <math>L</math> will always be infinite; if <math>\sigma</math> is finite then <math>|L|</math> will be [[Aleph-naught|<math>\aleph_0</math>]].

As the formal definition is inconvenient for everyday use, the definition of a specific signature is often abbreviated in an informal way, as in:

:"The standard signature for [[abelian group]]s is <math>\sigma = (+, -, 0),</math> where <math>-</math> is a unary operator."

Sometimes an algebraic signature is regarded as just a list of arities, as in:

:"The similarity type for abelian groups is <math>\sigma = (2, 1, 0).</math>"

Formally this would define the function symbols of the signature as something like <math>f_2</math> (which is binary), <math>f_1</math> (which is unary) and <math>f_0</math> (which is nullary), but in reality the usual names are used even in connection with this convention.

In [[mathematical logic]], very often symbols are not allowed to be nullary,{{Citation needed|date=January 2017}} so that constant symbols must be treated separately rather than as nullary function symbols. They form a set <math>S_{\operatorname{const}}</math> disjoint from <math>S_{\operatorname{func}},</math> on which the arity function <math>\operatorname{ar}</math> is not defined. However, this only serves to complicate matters, especially in proofs by induction over the structure of a formula, where an additional case must be considered. Any nullary relation symbol, which is also not allowed under such a definition, can be emulated by a unary relation symbol together with a sentence expressing that its value is the same for all elements. This translation fails only for empty structures (which are often excluded by convention). If nullary symbols are allowed, then every formula of [[propositional logic]] is also a formula of [[first-order logic]].

An example for an infinite signature uses <math>S_{\operatorname{func}} = \{+\} \cup \left\{f_a : a \in F\right\}</math> and <math>S_{\operatorname{rel}} = \{=\}</math> to formalize expressions and equations about a [[vector space]] over an infinite scalar field <math>F,</math> where each <math>f_a</math> denotes the unary operation of scalar multiplication by <math>a.</math> This way, the signature and the logic can be kept single-sorted, with vectors being the only sort.<ref>{{cite book | editor=James C. Abbot | title=Trends in Lattice Theory | location=Princeton/NJ | publisher=Van Nostrand | year=1967 | author=George Grätzer | authorlink=George Grätzer | contribution=IV. Universal Algebra | pages=173&ndash;210}} Here: p.173.</ref>

==Use of signatures in logic and algebra==

In the context of [[first-order logic]], the symbols in a signature are also known as the [[non-logical symbols]], because together with the logical symbols they form the underlying alphabet over which two [[formal language]]s are inductively defined: The set of ''terms'' over the signature and the set of (well-formed) ''formulas'' over the signature.

In a [[Structure (mathematical logic)|structure]], an ''interpretation'' ties the function and relation symbols to mathematical objects that justify their names: The interpretation of an <math>n</math>-ary function symbol <math>f</math> in a structure <math>\mathbf{A}</math> with ''domain'' <math>A</math> is a function <math>f^\mathbf{A} : A^n \to A,</math> and the interpretation of an <math>n</math>-ary relation symbol is a [[Finitary relation|relation]] <math>R^\mathbf{A} \subseteq A^n.</math> Here <math>A^n = A \times A \times \cdots \times A</math> denotes the <math>n</math>-fold [[cartesian product]] of the domain <math>A</math> with itself, and so <math>f</math> is in fact an <math>n</math>-ary function, and <math>R</math> an <math>n</math>-ary relation.

==Many-sorted signatures==

For many-sorted logic and for [[structure (mathematical logic)#Many-sorted structures|many-sorted structures]], signatures must encode information about the sorts. The most straightforward way of doing this is via '''{{visible anchor|symbol types}}''' that play the role of generalized arities.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070929131504/http://react.cs.uni-sb.de/%7Ezarba/snow/ch01.pdf Many-Sorted Logic], the first chapter in [https://web.archive.org/web/20081006212815/http://react.cs.uni-sb.de/~zarba/notes.html Lecture notes on Decision Procedures], written by [http://theory.stanford.edu/~zarba/ Calogero G. Zarba].</ref>

===Symbol types===

Let <math>S</math> be a set (of sorts) not containing the symbols <math>\times</math> or <math>\to.</math>

The symbol types over <math>S</math> are certain words over the alphabet <math>S \cup \{\times, \to\}</math>: the relational symbol types <math>s_1 \times \cdots \times s_n,</math> and the functional symbol types <math>s_1 \times \cdots \times s_n \to s^\prime,</math> for non-negative integers <math>n</math> and <math>s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n, s^\prime \in S.</math> (For <math>n = 0,</math> the expression <math>s_1 \times \cdots \times s_n</math> denotes the empty word.)

===Signature===

A (many-sorted) signature is a triple <math>(S, P, \operatorname{type})</math> consisting of
* a set <math>S</math> of sorts,
* a set <math>P</math> of symbols, and
* a map <math>\operatorname{type}</math> which associates to every symbol in <math>P</math> a symbol type over <math>S.</math>
